title: Display-fab panel interposers for wide-IO memory modules
idea: Use idle Gen-6 LCD lines (1.5-2 um lithography on large glass panels) to pattern multilayer redistribution interposers for wide, slow DRAM-to-processor links, replacing scarce silicon interposers.
why: Data movement (fact 5): wide-IO links at ~1 pJ/bit versus 10-20 pJ/bit for DDR5, and relief for the advanced-packaging bottleneck, using existing display capacity.

title: Acoustic-resonator frequency-division addressing replaces global predecoder buses
idea: Effect: mechanical (BAW/contour-mode) resonance. Give each subarray block an AlScN resonator tuned to a unique frequency (e.g., 64 tones from 1.0-2.6 GHz); the controller sends a tone burst on one shared line, and only the block whose resonator rings up past threshold enables its local wordline drivers. The address travels as a frequency instead of over dozens of routed wires.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): one RF line can replace ~20-40 global address/predecode wires and repeaters per bank.

title: Window-comparator sense amps flag uncertain bits as erasures
idea: Add a pair of offset-shifted comparators on the secondary sense path that flags bits whose sensed value fell inside a narrow uncertainty window; on-die ECC treats them as erasures, and erasure decoding corrects about 2x more bits than errors at unknown positions.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): tolerating ~2x more weak bits stretches refresh intervals ~2-4x using circuits old nodes already build.

title: Regenerative brakes: LC-resonant wordline drive returns wordline charge
idea: Like a hybrid car's brakes refilling the battery, connect the selected wordline through its driver to a bank-level spiral inductor so it swings to ~3 V resonantly from a tank capacitor, and on close let the charge ring back into the tank instead of dumping it to ground; the ~30%-efficient charge pump then only tops up losses.
why: Wordline and pump losses are ~15-25% of activation energy; ~85% recovery plus no pump overhead cuts that component ~10x; inductor ~0.05 mm2 per bank.

title: Zr: antiferroelectric zirconia flying capacitors shrink charge pumps
idea: Build charge-pump flying capacitors from antiferroelectric ZrO2, whose field-induced phase change stores ~3-5x the energy density of linear high-k at 2-3 V, operated inside the double-hysteresis window to pump VPP and VBB.
why: Pump capacitors are among the largest periphery blocks (fact 7); 3-5x denser caps cut pump area accordingly.

title: No matched analog pairs: delay-chain arbiter sense amps
idea: Limit: the sense amp must be synthesizable from standard digital cells. BL and BLB each set the supply of a short starved inverter chain, the cell's +/-dV becomes a ps-scale delay difference, and an SR-latch arbiter at the end decides; mismatch is trimmed by digitally tuned delay taps calibrated at power-up.
why: U.S. manufacturability and periphery cost: sense amps that port to any logic fab or node, with digital calibration replacing matched-pair area (SA area -30-40%).

title: Open-source CHIPS-funded DRAM periphery IP commons
idea: Scale up from company to nation: a federally funded, silicon-proven, royalty-free library of DRAM periphery blocks (sense amps, sub-wordline drivers, pumps, PHYs) on U.S. 28 nm processes, so a new U.S. entrant only has to develop arrays.
why: Cuts entrant design time ~2-3 years and ~$0.5B of cost (capital intensity, U.S. manufacturability).

title: Bottom-up Mo fill from Colorado moly replaces periphery tungsten
idea: Reverse fill direction and metal: periphery contacts, wordline straps and local interconnect are filled bottom-up by area-selective molybdenum CVD nucleating on the contact floor (no liner, no seams), with precursor refined from U.S.-mined molybdenum.
why: Tungsten chokepoint (China ~80%) removed; Mo's lower narrow-line resistance (~30-50%) speeds wordline drivers and drops liner steps.

title: Evict charge pumps: package PMIC supplies VPP to sixteen dies
idea: MINIFY on-die high-voltage generation to zero: one ~85%-efficient switched-inductor PMIC on the HBM base die or DIMM generates VPP/VBB for all dies and delivers them on dedicated TSVs or balls, replacing on-die capacitive pumps.
why: Facts 7 and 10: removes pump capacitors and oscillators (~3-5% of die) and raises VPP efficiency from ~30% to ~85%, cutting wall-plug wordline energy ~2.5x.

title: Wafer-scale memory board with pick-and-place replaceable cell tiles
idea: Ideal result: memory as a field of interchangeable tiles. A periphery interposer wafer carries all decoders and sense amps in repeated sockets; small cell-array tiles are compression-bonded, tested in place, and bad tiles are lifted and replaced.
why: Yield and capital (facts 4, 7): tiny tiles yield ~99%, and the periphery wafer can be built at 28-40 nm in the U.S.

title: Skip restore for read-once data like KV-cache streams
idea: MINIFY restore work: a read-and-forget command lets the SA latch the row without driving restore current back into the cells, and the controller marks the row invalid, for data consumed once (streamed activations, KV pages being evicted).
why: Fact 8: restore is ~40-50% of activation energy and time; skipping it raises effective bandwidth and reduces disturbance to neighbors.

title: Another dimension: stacked CFET sense amp fits a single bitline pitch
idea: TRIZ #17 Another dimension: the cross-coupled latch is built as complementary FETs stacked vertically (nFET pair under pFET pair with shared gates), so each sense amp fits one bitline pitch instead of two to four, letting every bitline of a 4F2 open-bitline array have its own amp.
why: Facts 4 and 7: sense-amp strip area ~-50% and 4F2 vertical-channel cells become usable, since their pitch cannot host today's planar sense amps.

title: Eliminate tungsten contact plugs with tall raised-epitaxy source/drain posts
idea: Pattern contact holes in an amorphous-carbon template with O2 plasma, then grow in-situ-doped Si:P/SiGe:B selective epitaxy (DCS/HCl/PH3/B2H6) up through them to ~80 nm, so the source/drain posts themselves reach M1. Ash the template and cap each post with NiSi.
why: Removes WF6 CVD and fluorocarbon contact etch for millions of periphery contacts, and with them tungsten (China ~80%) from the periphery.

title: Array cell capacitors as flying caps for on-die converters
idea: Wire blocks of spare and edge DRAM cell capacitors (very high density at ~5 fF each) into a multi-phase switched-capacitor converter that generates VPP, VBB and VARY at ~80-85% efficiency instead of ~30-40% for Dickson charge pumps.
why: Voltage floor and periphery (facts 10, 7): pumps take ~5% of die and waste power; doubling pump efficiency cuts wordline and refresh supply energy ~15-20%.

title: Electric-eel stacked charge pump built from spare array capacitors
idea: Electric eels stack thousands of electrocytes in series to reach 600 V. Build the VPP/VBB pumps from blocks of ordinary high-AR cell capacitors (dummy rows at mat edges, thousands in parallel), switched by array transistors into a series-parallel ladder stack, instead of planar MOS capacitors in the periphery.
why: Fact 7/10: pillar caps give ~50-100x more capacitance per area than planar caps. Pumps shrink ~5x (2-4% of die), and bigger flying caps raise pump efficiency ~1.5x.

title: Grid capacitor banks: dummy cell capacitors become pumps and decap
idea: Like a utility's capacitor bank, gang the edge/dummy rows of the cell array, whose high-AR capacitors are already built (~50 fF/um2), in parallel as charge-pump flying capacitors and on-die decoupling, replacing large planar MOS capacitors in the periphery.
why: Periphery area: MOS pump and decap area (~3-5% of die) shrinks ~10x by borrowing the densest capacitor on the chip.

title: Marx-generator local boost replaces the central VPP pump
idea: A 1924 Marx generator charges capacitors in parallel and switches them into series for a high-voltage spike. At each sub-wordline driver, three dummy cell capacitors charge to VDD in parallel during precharge and switch into series to deliver ~3 V only to the row being opened. The one added mask is a contact mask that strings them through existing array transistors.
why: Removes most of the central VPP charge pump and its global distribution (fact 7) and halves the VPP conversion loss (fact 10).

title: Glissando wordlines: stepwise adiabatic charging from tank capacitors
idea: A musician slides through notes instead of jumping. Ramp each wordline to 3 V in four steps from a ladder of on-die tank capacitors (built from spare cell capacitors) and return the charge to the tanks on the falling edge, instead of switching straight from the pump.
why: Stepwise charging cuts wordline CV^2 loss ~4x and avoids ~30%-efficient pump conversion, attacking the 3 V wordline energy floor (fact 10).

title: Ferroelectric-imbalanced sense latches keep open rows across power loss
idea: Constraint: open pages must survive an instant power cut with zero dump time. Two small HZO capacitors on each SA's internal nodes are polarized by the latched value in a ~10 ns pulse on power-fail detect (not on every activation, to spare endurance); when power returns, their remanent imbalance biases the latch so it re-resolves to the same value, recovering ~256 kB of open-row state.
why: Zero-latency persistence for in-flight rows (nvSRAM idea at row-buffer scale); complements a slower full-array backup.

title: Felted random-network decoder, mapped after manufacture
idea: Like felt made by matting random fibers instead of weaving, spray a sparse random network of nanowire switches between a few predecode lines and the wordline ends. Post-fab test discovers which address code reaches which wordline and stores the map in a small table, so no lithographically defined decoder is needed at wordline pitch.
why: Decoders for 3D-DRAM tiers and fine-pitch arrays are costly to pattern; a stochastic decoder needs no critical litho, cutting decoder area and masks ~50-80% for vertical stacks.

title: Eliminate the voltage-mode latch: selective-epitaxy bipolar pre-amp in bitline contact
idea: Form a vertical n-p-n inside each bitline contact by in-situ-doped selective epitaxy (DCS/HCl with PH3/B2H6, avoiding BF2 implants), with the bitline driving the base. The charge-share signal becomes a collector current (beta ~50) into one shared current comparator per 16 bitlines, and a shared write driver restores the cells.
why: Cuts SA latch count 16x (die -8-10%) with ~2 ns sensing, and drops fluorinated BF2 implant species from the periphery.

title: Pyroelectric read: wordline heat pulse makes polarization announce itself
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, and the read must not flip domains. A ~1 ns current pulse through a resistive wordline strap heats one row of ferroelectric capacitors by ~10 K; each cell emits a pyroelectric current whose sign matches its polarization, and charge integrators on the bitlines read it without ever crossing the coercive field.
why: Non-destructive NV read with no reference cells (sign detection). Risk: ns thermal time constants and the ~fJ heating energy per bit.

title: Physarum flux-reinforcement floorplanner for global data and command buses
idea: The slime mould Physarum thickens tubes that carry flow and prunes the rest, finding near-optimal networks. Its flux-reinforcement model drives the routing of a DRAM die's global data, command and test buses, weighted by real access traces. Software only, ~$400k over 18 months, released and licensed.
why: Fact 5/7: trace-weighted Physarum topologies can cut weighted global wirelength ~10-20%, with similar savings in internal data-movement energy and bus area.

title: Ferroelectric coercive-edge capacitor avalanches tiny bitline signals
idea: 1950s ferroelectric memories failed because switching was too easy to trigger; this turns that flaw into gain. One block mask keeps an HZO capacitor at each sense node, biased just below its coercive voltage. A 30-50 mV bitline signal tips it into switching, which dumps ~20 µC/cm² of polarization charge into the latch, and the capacitor is reset each cycle. Wear is spread across redundant capacitors.
why: ~10x charge gain at the sense node lets Cs fall toward 1-2 fF (fact 1 charge wall) with no new cell physics.

title: Excessive action: multi-row activation sums redundant copies in weak mats
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial or excessive action: in mats with weak cells or high temperature the controller writes each bit into 2-4 rows sharing the same bitlines and later opens them together so their charges sum on the bitline, trading capacity for 2-4x signal instead of scrapping the die or raising refresh.
why: Facts 1 and 3: dies with weak tails sell at reduced capacity instead of being scrapped (yield ~+5-15%), and refresh in redundant mode can drop ~4x.

title: LCD overdrive pre-emphasis speeds slow thin-film bitlines
idea: Borrowed from LCD response-time overdrive: column drivers apply a brief over-voltage pulse sized by a lookup table of previous and target state, so slow 20-40 cm2/Vs oxide-TFT bitlines and wordlines settle in about a third of the time.
why: Speed: moves glass-panel memory from ~100 ns toward ~30-40 ns cycles without high-mobility channels.

title: Avalanche-gain bitline preamp borrowed from failed impact-ionization MOS
idea: Failure mined: I-MOS (the impact-ionization MOSFET) died as a logic switch from high voltage and hot-carrier damage over billions of cycles. Fix: make a gated p-i-n avalanche preamp the first sensing stage, firing once per activation for ~1 ns and multiplying the cell's charge-share signal 10-30x before a conventional latch. Its duty cycle is ~1e-4 of logic use.
why: Charge wall (fact 1): cell capacitance can drop 5-10x (to ~0.5-1 fF), allowing planar or short capacitors and easing 3D DRAM (fact 2).

title: Chemotaxis run-and-tumble firmware harvesting per-bank timing guardband
idea: E. coli keeps running while conditions improve and tumbles when they worsen. Controller firmware nudges a bank's tRCD/tRP/tRAS down one clock at random and keeps the change while ECC scrubs and canary rows stay clean (run). It reverts and re-randomizes on any corrected error (tumble), tracking temperature and aging. About $500k of firmware and FPGA validation over 18 months.
why: Commodity timings carry 20-40% guardband. Harvesting ~20% lower latency adaptively raises useful bandwidth per DIMM, so fewer DIMMs serve a workload.

title: Bubble swap-gate sense amps exchange two rows in one cycle
idea: Bubble memories used swap gates to trade a bit between a minor loop and the major loop in one operation. Give each sense amp a second small latch: one activation senses row A into latch 1, the next senses row B into latch 2, and each is restored into the other's row. Two rows swap in two activations without data leaving the chip.
why: Makes in-DRAM row migration cheap for row-hammer mitigation (fact 9) and hot/cold placement, replacing large TRR counter tables with swap-based remapping at ~10x lower mitigation energy.

title: 77 K memory pods: cold sensing permits flat capacitors and tiers
idea: Failure mined: the Microsoft-Rambus cryo-DRAM program was shelved because cooling general servers cost more than it saved. Fix: target AI clusters that already run liquid-nitrogen loops. At 77 K leakage falls by >1e6 (refresh nearly vanishes), kT/C noise and SA offset fall ~2-4x and bitline resistance falls ~6x, so a 0.4 fF planar MIM cell is enough and can be stacked in deposited tiers.
why: 10x at the same cost: replacing the 70:1 capacitor (fact 1) with flat cells allows 16-24 litho-shared tiers (~10x bits/mm^2). Cooling energy is offset by the eliminated refresh and lower I^2R losses.

title: Sense-amp latches drive silicon-photonic rings, skipping column decode
idea: Reverse the data path: instead of SA -> column mux -> global I/O -> PHY, groups of SA latches directly drive micro-ring modulators on a silicon-photonics layer from a U.S. photonics fab (e.g., New York), bonded over the array, with 64 wavelengths per waveguide carrying the row out.
why: Fact 5: data movement ~1 pJ/bit vs 3-20 pJ/bit; the global I/O tree (~5-8% of periphery) disappears.

title: PRML read channel undoes bitline crosstalk instead of shielding
idea: Port the partial-response maximum-likelihood detection IBM introduced for magnetic disks in 1990. Groups of 8 adjacent bitlines are sampled by 3-bit flash comparators after charge sharing, and a small Viterbi detector decides the bits jointly using the die's measured coupling matrix. Inter-bitline crosstalk becomes a modeled channel instead of noise that has to be shielded or twisted away.
why: Allows ~30% tighter bitline pitch or ~40% less signal margin (facts 1, 4), trading a little periphery logic for array density.

title: Solar epitaxial lift-off: periphery layer on a reused donor wafer
idea: High-efficiency III-V solar cells peel their thin active layer off a GaAs substrate that is reused many times. Grow the periphery CMOS device layer on a porous-silicon release layer, bond it to the array wafer, split it off, and re-epi the donor 10+ times instead of consuming a fresh prime wafer for the periphery tier.
why: Water and scarce resources: crystal-growth and wafering (slice, lap, polish, clean) water per periphery tier falls ~10x, and so does Spruce Pine quartz-crucible demand for that tier.

title: Nano vacuum-channel transistors as radiation-proof wordline boost drivers
idea: Nuclear and EMP environments favor vacuum electronics; field-emission vacuum-channel transistors with ~50 nm gaps defined by oxide etch-back rather than lithography switch 3-5 V wordlines with no gate-oxide stress and full immunity to heat and radiation.
why: Shrinks high-voltage SWD devices (fact 7) and lifts the wordline voltage ceiling; emitter reliability is speculative.

title: Hospital plasma sterilization: radical-based pre-gate clean for periphery
idea: Hospitals swapped steam autoclaves for hydrogen-peroxide plasma sterilizers. Replace the RCA wet sequence before the periphery high-k/metal-gate stack with remote hydrogen-radical organic/metal removal plus anhydrous HF/alcohol vapor oxide etch in one vacuum chamber.
why: Water: RCA SC1/SC2/HF with cascaded rinses (~50-100 L UPW per full clean) is the classic water hog; the dry radical sequence cuts ~10x across the ~4-6 periphery pre-gate/pre-diffusion cleans.

title: Murray's-law tapered power-tree generator for DRAM periphery
idea: Blood vessels and leaf veins follow Murray's law (parent radius^3 = sum of children's), minimizing transport cost per volume. An open-source EDA plugin synthesizes periphery VDD/VPP/VSS distribution as Murray-tapered trees instead of uniform meshes, with IR-drop sign-off on a test layout. Two engineers plus licenses, ~$600k in 24 months, then licensed to DRAM/eDRAM teams.
why: Fact 7 + tungsten chokepoint: ~20-30% less periphery power metal at equal IR drop frees routing tracks and cuts W/Cu usage in the lower levels.

title: Chess clock: time-domain race arbiter replaces voltage latch sense amp
idea: Turn voltage into time like a chess clock: the bitline and reference each set the current of a starved inverter discharging a node, and a mutual-exclusion arbiter (first press locks out the other) latches whichever crosses first before a restore driver writes back.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10) and SA area: delay gain turns ~20 mV into ~100 ps and keeps working at 0.5-0.6 V where cross-coupled latches fail; the arbiter is ~4 transistors plus 2 delay cells.

title: Hot-carrier-injection trimming nulls sense-amp offset permanently at test
idea: Effect: hot-carrier charge trapping. At wafer test, a built-in ramp measures each SA's offset, then short high-Vds pulses inject hot carriers into the stronger transistor's gate oxide to raise its Vt until the pair balances within ~3 mV; the trapped charge holds for years, with an optional field top-up.
why: SA area (fact 7): offset sets SA sizing (Pelgrom), so cutting sigma from ~15 mV to ~3 mV allows ~4-10x smaller SA devices or 2x cells per bitline.

title: Pre-printed forms: sea-of-gates periphery personalized by two i-line metal masks
idea: Like printers who stock pre-printed letterhead and add only the name, fab one universal 180 nm periphery master with gate-array sites for pumps, decoders and control. Interface width, protocol (DDR/LPDDR/CXL-lite) and redundancy are personalized with just two metal masks, the 1990s ASIC gate-array method.
why: Cuts per-variant mask sets and NRE ~80-90%, so small U.S. fabs can serve many memory SKUs from one wafer inventory.

title: Flemish-bond stacking: staggered tiers share each sense-amp strip vertically
idea: Like bricks laid in Flemish bond so joints never line up, offset alternate 3D-DRAM tiers by half a mat. Every SA strip then sits between the bitline ends of the tier above and the tier below and serves both through short vertical vias.
why: Halves SA strips per bit in 3D DRAM, attacking the periphery overhead behind the ~26-tier break-even; break-even tier count could fall ~20-30%.

title: Instant-photography dry resist and dry develop for periphery litho
idea: Like Polaroid replacing the wet darkroom, vapor-deposit a metal-oxide photoresist, expose, develop it in a plasma/thermal gas step and strip it dry on every periphery-only mask (implant blocks, contacts, metals), so these layers never touch developer, rinse or wet strip.
why: Water: track develop/rinse and post-implant wet strips (~15-25 L UPW per layer) fall ~10x on periphery layers; resist solvent supply chains shrink too.

title: Shift-register row sequencer replaces decoders in streaming banks
idea: MINIFY the row decoder in designated stream banks to a circular shift register that advances one wordline per ACT plus a coarse 1-of-16 jump decoder, since AI weight and KV streams open rows in order; random traffic is steered to normal banks.
why: Fact 7: decoder area -80% and decode energy -70% in stream banks; ~5-8% die saved if half the banks stream.

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM with cryo-tuned long-bitline sense amps
idea: Box: smaller cap x Si access x cryo-optimized SA x LN2-immersed module x bulk Si x standard fab. At 77 K the subthreshold slope falls to ~20 mV/dec and mismatch narrows, so SAs resolve smaller signals; bitlines grow 4x and retention reaches hours, removing most refresh logic.
why: SA count /4 (periphery ~-20%) and refresh ~0; energy per bit lower even after cooling overhead in large AI pods.

title: Dual-threshold margin sensing sets each row's own refresh interval
idea: Like event cameras that report only changes: during refresh, a second coarse comparator in each SA stripe flags whether any cell in the row came in below a 'healthy' margin window. Healthy rows skip the next 1-3 refresh rounds; only flagged rows keep the base rate, driven by measured margin instead of a static profile.
why: Refresh operations cut ~60-80% because most cells retain >1 s, recovering fact 3's 10-20% bandwidth; adapts to temperature and aging automatically.

title: Model-ROM DIMMs hold frozen weights with DRAM interfaces
idea: Time jump to model-release cadence: inference weights frozen for months are written once into via- or antifuse-programmed ROM mats that reuse DRAM-style sense amps and the DDR/LPDDR interface, and modules are recycled when the model retires.
why: Weights are ~60-80% of inference memory; capacitor-free ~4F2 ROM cells need zero refresh (fact 3), give ~3x density (fact 1) and skip capacitor EUV/HAR steps (fact 4).

title: Second-harmonic polarization read makes FeRAM non-destructive
idea: Failure mined: Ramtron FeRAM's read switched the ferroelectric, causing fatigue and imprint and forcing a write-back on every read. Fix: apply a sub-coercive sine (~0.2 Vc) and detect the phase of the second harmonic of the displacement current with a phase-sensitive sense amp. The nonlinear permittivity is asymmetric, so the harmonic's sign follows the polarization direction without switching it.
why: Removes destructive read and restore energy (fact 8, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit) and read-induced fatigue, pushing ferroelectric cells toward unlimited read endurance.

title: Dairy-cooperative periphery foundry co-owned by rival DRAM makers
idea: Like farmer co-ops that share one creamery, DRAM vendors jointly own a U.S. fab that makes only periphery/CMOS-under-array logic wafers to a common bond interface. Each vendor bonds its proprietary array wafers on top and buys periphery at cost.
why: Pools capex for the ~49%-of-die periphery function, frees each vendor's DRAM-node capacity for cells (~1.5x bits per DRAM wafer), and puts a large memory fab in the U.S.

title: 1T-8C ferroelectric stack: plate-line selection and twin-plate reference sensing
idea: Failure mined: Ramtron's FeRAM never shrank because each bit needed its own transistor (1T1C, often 2T2C). Fix: stack 8 HZO capacitors vertically on one access transistor's storage node, each on its own plate line, and read one by pulsing its plate while the other 7 float. A twin dummy plate provides a matched reference that cancels coupling from the unselected capacitors on the shared node.
why: 10x at the same cost: 8 bits per transistor on a ~4F^2 vertical-channel footprint = ~12x bits/mm^2, with all 8 capacitors made from one deposition stack and one hole etch.

title: Two-device sense amp: Esaki tunnel-diode Goto pair latch
idea: Limit: a sense amp may contain only two devices. Use a series pair of Si/SiGe Esaki tunnel diodes (a 1960s Goto pair) whose N-shaped I-V gives the shared node two stable points; a clocked bias ramp drives the node through its unstable point, and the +/-50 mV bitline nudge decides which stable state it falls into within ~50 ps.
why: Periphery area and speed: 2 devices instead of the 6-10 in an offset-compensated latch, which could cut the SA stripe by ~3x. Matching depends on peak current rather than Vt, so random dopant mismatch matters less; decisions cost sub-fJ.

title: Universality: sense amps chain into shift register, deleting column decoders
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: after a row is latched, each sense amp also acts as one stage of a two-phase shift register (two extra transistors couple neighbours), streaming the page out of one edge port. Column decoders, column-select lines and most local I/O wiring disappear; random columns are reached by pipelined skip-shifting.
why: Fact 7: removes column decoders and CSL drivers (~8-12% of die) at the cost of extra latency for far columns; a natural fit for sequential AI tensor streaming.

title: BTI-balanced sense latches through epoch-wise data polarity swapping
idea: At 125 C, NBTI/PBTI shifts Vt ~10-30 mV over 10 years, mostly on whichever latch half sees one data value more often, eating a ~50 mV signal. Store every row inverted on alternate refresh epochs (one polarity bit per row) and swap which SA half is 'true', so both halves age equally to within ~1 mV.
why: Keeps sense margin intact for 10 y at 125 C without guardband; lets Cs stay ~20% smaller than an aging-guardbanded design (fact 1).

title: Eliminate per-column sense amps: charge-coupled shift readout to edge amplifier
idea: Under each row of storage nodes, run a buried-channel CCD register. On read, all cell charges of the row dump into the CCD and are clocked sideways (4-phase, ~1 GHz) to one floating-diffusion amplifier per 1,024 columns, which digitizes them in series. Restore uses reverse clocking.
why: Removes the SA stripes (-10-15% of die) for a bulk sequential tier. At 0.99999 transfer efficiency per stage, ~1% of the charge is lost over 1,024 stages, and a full row takes ~1 us, which suits weights and checkpoints but not random access.

title: Scout comparators forward speculative data before the sense amp settles
idea: Inverting 'data is valid only after the latch fully resolves': a tiny scout comparator on each selected column taps the bitlines through high-impedance gates at ~60% of tRCD and forwards data early, while the main sense amp keeps developing and restoring normally; a parity check on the scout word triggers a replay from the main latch on mismatch.
why: First-data latency -25-30% for ~1% added periphery area, because only the 64-512 selected columns get scouts; replay rate is tuned by scout timing.

title: Aerosol-jet printed edge wiring connects staircase-stacked memory dies
idea: Worse: drill TSVs through every HBM die. Flip: stack dies in an offset staircase with printed insulating ramps and aerosol-jet-print signal and power traces down the exposed edges, connecting pads tier to tier with no through-silicon vias.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): no TSV keep-out area or TSV yield loss; cheaper stacking for capacity tiers.

title: LCD gate-on-array shift registers replace row decoders
idea: Borrowed from LCD gate-on-array scanning: rows in streaming banks are selected by a token passed down a compact shift register (one 4-6 transistor stage per wordline), exactly as panels scan gate lines. Random access stays in a smaller decoded side bank.
why: Periphery: row-decoder and predecode area down ~60-70% in banks serving sequential weight and KV-cache streams.

title: Two-threshold sensing turns every read into a retention health check
idea: Ideal result: refresh only the bits that are truly about to fail. Every Nth activation, the SA stripe fires against a second, offset reference that flags cells whose signal is within 30% of failing; the controller logs those rows for faster refresh and stretches refresh for the healthy majority.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3): measures the leakage tail in the field instead of guarding for it; 60-80% fewer refreshes, reclaiming most of 16-33% idle power and 10-20% bandwidth.

title: Light-driven wordlines turn the decoder into an optical pattern
idea: Ideal result: addressing at light speed with no decoder transistors. A photonic layer above the array carries waveguides with grating taps over each sub-wordline driver; a photoconductive switch fires the driver only when its waveguide-wavelength pair is lit, with decoding done by an off-array laser and arrayed-waveguide router.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and energy: row decoders and global wordline wiring shrink to waveguides; fJ-class addressing energy.

title: Radar time-of-flight addressing with counter-propagating pulses
idea: Like a phased array placing energy where waves meet, launch two short pulses into opposite ends of a row-select transmission line; their launch delay sets where they overlap, and only there does the summed amplitude exceed the row-driver threshold. A 512-row decoder becomes two pulse generators and a digital delay.
why: Periphery area: decoders shrink ~10x, if ~10 ps on-die timing and dispersion can be controlled.

title: Stepwise wordline charging from cell-capacitor tank banks
idea: Revive 1990s adiabatic stepwise charging. Each wordline rises to 3 V in 6 steps through switches to tank capacitors held at intermediate voltages and falls back through them, recovering most of its CV² energy. The tanks are dummy DRAM cell-capacitor arrays reused in the periphery, so the only added mask is a block mask that opens the storage-node module there.
why: Wordline switching energy falls ~4-6x despite the 3 V floor (fact 10). Area cost is near zero because cell capacitors give ~100 fF/µm².

title: Stepwise adiabatic bitline charging from on-die tank rails
idea: Inverting 'the charge for each bitline swing is thrown away': bitlines are restored in four steps through intermediate rails held by large on-die tank capacitors, which are refilled when bitlines precharge back, so each swing dissipates about 1/N of the usual CV^2/2.
why: Bitline/array energy -50-70% for a few ns of extra restore time; attacks the CV^2 voltage-floor wall without lowering voltages.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging from a tank-capacitor ladder
idea: Time-stretch the wordline edge from ~1 ns to ~5 ns and charge it in 6 voltage steps from a ladder of deep-trench tank capacitors on the periphery wafer that recapture the charge when the wordline falls, so each 3 V wordline is charged quasi-adiabatically instead of straight from the VPP pump.
why: Wordline CV^2 at ~3 V plus ~30-40%-efficient pumps are stuck at the voltage floor (fact 10); stepwise charging cuts wordline+pump energy ~4-5x, about 10-15% of activation energy, for a few ns of tRCD.

title: Image sensor run backward: pinned-diode memory with floating-diffusion readout
idea: Reverse the pixel: in a U.S. CMOS image-sensor fab, a 4T pixel's fully depleted pinned photodiode stores electrically injected charge instead of photo-charge; reading is complete transfer to a floating diffusion and a source follower onto the column with correlated double sampling, and reverse transfer restores the bit.
why: Fact 3: pinned-diode dark current gives seconds-scale retention (~100x less refresh); fact 1: no tall capacitor and a gain-buffered readout. ~10-14F2 cells suit energy-bound tiers.

title: Fiber-optic EDFA-style in-line repeaters along long bitlines
idea: Like optical amplifiers spaced along long-haul fiber, insert a tiny IGZO TFT preamp/isolation switch in the BEOL every 128 cells, buffering each local segment's signal onto a global bitline, so one silicon SA serves an 8x longer bitline.
why: Periphery area: SA stripes shrink ~4-8x (~15-20% of die to ~4%); segmenting also cuts bitline C, raising signal per fF of Cs.

title: Otoacoustic diagnostics: supply-current spectra reveal DRAM sense margin
idea: Healthy cochleae emit faint sounds that allow non-invasive hearing tests. Standard activate/read bursts run while a fast shunt samples DIMM supply current. The spectral shape of sense-amp and restore transients exposes weak banks, timing margin and aging without vendor test modes. A $20k scope plus an ML classifier trained on 1,000 DIMMs, ~$400k in 18 months.
why: Supply axis: grades used and salvaged DRAM in seconds instead of hours of pattern testing, and sets per-DIMM refresh/timing.

title: Delay-line wave-pipelined data bus on one thick RDL layer
idea: Mercury delay lines stored bits as pulses in flight. One added thick-copper redistribution layer, which reuses existing pad openings as vias, carries low-loss global data lines with 3-4 bits in flight at once (wave pipelining, used in 1960s IBM machines) and no intermediate pipeline latches or repeaters.
why: Triples global-bus throughput per wire, removes repeater and latch stripes (fact 7) and cuts global-data energy ~30% (fact 5).

title: LCD-line excimer laser crystallizes poly-Si periphery above the array
idea: Borrow the 1990s LTPS LCD backplane process: deposit a-Si over the finished array, then crystallize it with excimer-laser pulses that melt only the top ~50 nm while the array stays below ~400 C. Build 180 nm-rule periphery (pumps, predecoders, control) in that layer and wire it down to the array.
why: Periphery-over-array with legacy tools reclaims ~30-40% of die area; LTPS mobility (~100-300 cm^2/Vs) is enough for logic that does not need to match bitline pitch.

title: Homeostatic body bias: replica latch steers sense-amp wells
idea: Living cells hold their internal state steady by feedback. A replica sense amp per bank measures its own offset continuously, and a slow loop adjusts the NMOS and PMOS well bias of the whole SA stripe to null systematic drift from temperature and NBTI aging.
why: Systematic drift is ~30-40% of the SA guard band; nulling it lets SA devices shrink or bitlines lengthen (fact 7).

title: Triple-row charge sharing detects duplicate pages for in-DRAM dedup
idea: Effect: multi-row charge-sharing majority. On commodity DDR4/DDR5, an FPGA controller issues back-to-back ACTs (the timing-violation trick from ComputeDRAM) to open a candidate page, a complement copy of the suspected twin and an all-zero reference together; the result equals the reference wherever the pages agree. Duplicate 8 KB rows are found at sense-amp bandwidth and mapped to one physical copy.
why: Usable supply: VM and AI-serving memory often holds 10-30% duplicate pages (zero pages, shared weights, KV prefixes); cheap in-DRAM comparison enables continuous dedup worth ~+10-25% effective capacity.

title: Po: decoders woven into wiring — a-Si diode matrix
idea: Po: a decoder made of wire crossings. Build the row predecoder as a 1960s-style diode matrix, with hydrogenated amorphous-silicon p-i-n diodes deposited at the crossings of two BEOL aluminum levels above the array, so decoding uses metal-layer space instead of silicon area.
why: Periphery (#7) and capital (#4): moves ~3-5% of die (predecode) off silicon using Si and H deposited below 350 C on cheap tools.

title: Inductive coil links replace signal TSVs in memory stacks
idea: Worse: drill thousands of signal TSVs through every die and lose area and yield. Flip: put small spiral coils in top metal for near-field inductive data links between thinned stacked dies, keeping only a few large power TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): signal-TSV keep-out area and much TSV-related yield loss removed.

title: Stepwise adiabatic wordline charging with on-die tank capacitors
idea: Charging C through a switch to V always dissipates CV^2/2; charging in N equal steps from N-1 tank capacitors dissipates ~CV^2/(2N). Drive the 3 V wordlines and bitline restore in 4 steps from tank capacitors built in the array's own capacitor process.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): wordline/restore energy ~3-4x lower; charge-pump load and area drop too.

title: Tire retreading: CXL rehab buffer gives retired DRAM second life
idea: Truck fleets retread tires instead of buying new. Sell a CXL memory-expander buffer chip whose periphery profiles retired DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs in situ (per-row retention margin, weak-column sensing), applies per-region refresh rates and column remaps, and pools them as tier-2 memory under strong ECC, fed by hyperscaler decommissioning streams.
why: Water/supply: a reused GB avoids essentially all of its manufacturing water (>10x vs new) and adds supply with no fab; large volumes of retired DRAM are shredded today.

title: Hybrid-bonded area pads above each bank replace the global datapath
idea: Worse: haul every bit across the die through global I/O lines and serializers to edge pads. Flip: place hybrid-bonded area-array pads directly above each bank's column logic so a logic die below reads each bank locally, deleting global I/O buses and most serializers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5) and periphery area (fact 7): <1 pJ/bit access and ~8-10% of die freed.

title: Deuterium re-passivation anneal shrinks leakage tail of reject dies
idea: Effect: hydrogen-isotope passivation of Si/SiO2 dangling bonds (Pb centers). Bare reject DRAM dies or thinned wafers are annealed in a small tube furnace in 5-10% D2 at ~350-400 C; deuterium re-passivates the traps in junction depletion regions whose SRH generation current dominates the retention tail, and the dies are re-screened before resale.
why: Refresh/yield (fact 3): if tail leakage halves, retention-fail dies become sellable and refresh can relax; furnace capex <$0.5M.

title: Dynamics: sense amps switch to two-bit multilevel mode when cool
idea: TRIZ #15 Dynamics: each sense amp adds a second time-staggered latch and a mid-reference so a mat can run either 1-bit robust mode or 2-bit-per-cell multilevel mode; the controller enables multilevel on mats whose thermal sensor and retention telemetry show margin (cool, cold data) and migrates data out when temperature rises.
why: Density: ~1.6-2x bits per cell on cool, cold data, with capacity that flexes with conditions; Fact 1's small charge sets the risk.

title: Persistence-domain DRAM standard: mandatory per-die power-fail dump pin
idea: Constraint: data survives power loss in every server, by standard. Propose a JEDEC/OCP 'DDR-P' profile in which each die has a power-fail pin, an energy-budget register and an in-die backup engine, so hosts can drop batteries, NVDIMM-N modules and flash-backed caches; seed it via U.S. federal procurement of persistent memory.
why: Strategy: creates a market for NV periphery IP in which U.S. firms can lead, and removes ~$50-100 of backup hardware per server.

title: Mixed mat: fast floating-body and nonvolatile FeFET share sense amps
idea: Inverting 'one array holds one cell type': alternate rows in a mat are floating-body (fast, volatile) and FeFET (nonvolatile), both read by drain current, and one dual-mode current sense amp switches bias between them so hot data and persistent data live in the same mat.
why: Gives a hot tier and a no-refresh tier for the cost of one periphery, cutting refresh power for cold data ~90%.

title: BEOL oxide-TFT sense amps above NV crossbar: die equals array
idea: Constraint: NV crossbar cells (BEOL-compatible MRAM/ReRAM/FTJ). Build the sense amps, column muxes and local drivers from complementary oxide TFTs (n-IGZO plus p-SnO or Te) in the BEOL directly above or between crossbar tiers, so the front-end silicon under the array holds only global logic.
why: Periphery 49% (fact 7): die area per bit approaches the array area (~2x density); BEOL processing at <=400 C suits U.S. legacy fabs.

title: Chopper-swapped multi-decision latch averaging beneath offset
idea: Time-slice one read: the isolated SA latch fires 8 times in ~1.5 ns on the same held bitline signal, swapping its inputs on alternate decisions, and a 3-bit counter takes the majority, so fixed offset cancels and noise averages out.
why: Effective offset ~5x lower keeps reads correct at ~1/3 the signal: ~2x lower Cs or 2x longer bitlines (facts 1, 7).

title: Merging: wordline driver doubles as analog row-hammer activation counter
idea: TRIZ #5 Merging: each sub-wordline driver gets a tiny pumped capacitor that gains a fixed charge packet on every activation and leaks with a ~32 ms time constant; when it crosses a Schmitt threshold the driver flags its two neighbours for targeted refresh. Counting is merged into the device that already sees every activation.
why: Fact 9: deterministic per-row protection at ~1k-activation thresholds for ~2-4% area, instead of 10-20% SRAM/CAM tracking overhead in the controller or die, with no bandwidth spent on blind refresh.

title: Al: anodic alumina nanopore forests as litho-free die-to-die vias
idea: Anodize an aluminum layer to self-order 20-40 nm pores, electroplate Cu into them, and use the vertical wire forest as a dense random interconnect between a stacked periphery die and the array; a calibration pass learns which pores join which pads.
why: Gives ~1e9-1e10 vertical connections per cm2 without EUV/ArF or tight bond alignment, enabling periphery-on-top stacking (fact 7) cheaper than TSVs (fact 6).

title: Self-restoring floating-body read deletes the write-back path
idea: Inverting 'a read disturbs the cell and needs restore circuitry': floating-body cells are read with drain bias just into impact ionization, so a '1' cell regenerates its own body holes through bipolar gain while a '0' cell stays empty, making every read a self-refresh.
why: Removes write-back drivers and restore timing from the column periphery, cuts read energy ~30%, and makes hot rows refresh themselves.

title: Immune patrol: margin sweep on a test row during REF
idea: An immune system samples for threats constantly. During each REF command the die spends a few ns reading a reserved per-bank test row at a slightly shifted precharge level and keeps a running estimate of the best VBLP, re-centering the sense eye as cells and SAs age.
why: Recovers ~10-20 mV of guard band (fact 1) and spots weakening banks early; REF already exists, so nothing changes on the bus.

title: AM radio dial: frequency-multiplexed resonator readout of 64 bitlines
idea: Like superconducting-qubit dispersive readout or an AM dial, give each of 64 bitlines a tiny BEOL LC resonator at its own frequency, all coupled to one feedline; the post-charge-sharing bitline voltage tunes a varactor and shifts its resonance by a few MHz. One broadband comb probe plus a digital channelizer reads all 64 at once, and a minimal pass-gate driver writes the decoded value back.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): replaces 64 full latch sense amps with one wideband receiver plus 64 write-back switches, potentially 3-5x less SA-strip area if resonators fit in upper metal over the array.

title: Frequency-multiplexed resonator readout of 64 bitlines per receiver
idea: Box: trench cap x cryo-CMOS access x frequency-division readout x interposer-integrated resonators x sapphire-on-Si x high-Tc superconducting film. At 77 K each bitline ends in a high-Q LC resonator at a unique frequency whose varactor is detuned by the shared cell charge; one broadband LNA plus FFT reads 64 bitlines at once, like kinetic-inductance detector arrays.
why: Replaces 64 SAs with one receiver (SA area -90% for cryo data-center memory); cryo also stretches retention to minutes.

title: Qubit-style dispersive resonator readout of a varactor storage node
idea: Quantum computers read qubits non-destructively through a tiny shift in resonator frequency; a cell's storage node biases a MOS varactor that loads a shared bitline resonator, and a microwave probe reads the state as a phase shift without discharging the node. Read needs no restore cycle.
why: Removes fact 8's destructive read and restore energy and allows repeated reads of one row; speculative because the per-cell capacitance shift is tiny.

title: Sprue-and-runner test periphery: built in scribe lanes, sawn off at dicing
idea: Like the sprues and runners trimmed off a molded part, put test-mode logic, compressed-test comparators, extra probe pads and fuse-programming drivers in the 80-100 um scribe lanes at 180 nm rules, linked across the seal ring by sacrificial connections. After wafer sort and repair, the dicing saw removes them.
why: Recovers the ~3-5% of die area spent on test-only periphery: a direct ~4% bits-per-wafer gain with no process change.

title: Ti: titanium-oxo resist and 213 nm solid-state laser lithography
idea: Pattern periphery layers with a Ti-oxo-cluster photoresist exposed by a fifth-harmonic Nd:YAG 213 nm solid-state laser scanner instead of ArF/KrF excimers, whose gas fills are mostly neon plus argon or krypton; the Ti-O resist doubles as its own hardmask, dropping an argon-sputtered layer.
why: Removes the neon and krypton dependence from periphery patterning; periphery pitches of ~40-60 nm are reachable; ~20% fewer hardmask steps (fact 4).

title: Retina lateral inhibition between neighboring sense amplifiers
idea: Copying the retina's horizontal cells, each sense amp gets weak cross-coupled 'inhibition' transistors to its two neighbors, so a disturbance common to the region (wordline kick, plate bounce, aggressor-bitline coupling) is subtracted before latching while the true local difference survives.
why: Cancels the correlated noise that eats ~30-40% of the sense budget, allowing 1024 cells per bitline (half the SA stripes, ~7% die) or ~30% less cell charge (facts 1, 7).

title: Seebeck heat-flux sensors predict die temperature to drop refresh guardbands
idea: Effect: Seebeck thermopile heat-flux sensing plus package thermal lag. Laminate off-the-shelf thin-film Bi2Te3 heat-flux sensors between DRAM packages and the heat spreader; heat flux leads die temperature by tens of ms through the package's thermal RC, so the controller forecasts temperature ~50 ms ahead and runs relaxed refresh until a real rise is coming.
why: Refresh (fact 3): removing a static ~10 C guardband gives ~2x longer refresh at typical temperatures (~30-40% refresh energy) with module-level parts.

title: Swap voltage-amplitude sensing for time-to-digital bitline sensing
idea: Substitute the voltage-amplitude latch with a time-domain sensor: the shared bitline charge sets the bias of a current-starved delay cell, and one 8-way time-to-digital arbiter shared by 8 bitline pairs decides which edge arrives first. Signal margin becomes picoseconds of delay instead of millivolts on a latch.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): pitch-matched latches shrink about 4x because the TDC sits off-pitch and is shared; tolerates 30-40% lower bitline swing, easing the Cs charge wall (fact 1).

title: Time-domain sensing via bitline-starved delay elements
idea: Convert the tiny bitline difference into a delay difference: the true and complement bitlines each set the current of a starved inverter chain, and a digital arbiter decides which edge arrives first, with a vernier for extra resolution. The SA becomes digital logic that scales with logic nodes.
why: Periphery area and voltage (facts 7, 10): SA shrinks and runs at core voltage; delay averaging over several stages reduces offset ~sqrt(N).

title: Time-domain sense amps race delay lines at 0.6 V arrays
idea: Worse: insist on full 1 V voltage swings and amplitude margin on every bitline. Flip: let the bitline differential set the bias of two current-starved delay stages and resolve which edge arrives first with a time comparator, so a ~0.6 V array supply still yields a clean decision.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): bitline CV^2 energy drops ~60% if VARY goes from 1.0 to 0.6 V, with less access-transistor stress.

title: Alien race-to-latch: delay-domain sensing with shared arbiters
idea: An alien that measures everything in time converts each bitline pair's small differential into a delay difference through two current-starved inverters, and a 4-transistor mutual-exclusion arbiter decides which edge arrived first; one arbiter serves 4 bitlines by staggered firing.
why: Delay-domain comparison keeps working at low supply, enabling VARY ~0.6 V instead of ~1 V (fact 10) with fewer analog transistors per bitline (fact 7).

title: Mayfly memory: refresh-free banks for data that dies young
idea: Adult mayflies live a day and have no working gut, so no maintenance organs for a short life. An allocator flag marks 'ephemeral' pages (AI activations, KV scratch, network buffers) that are rewritten within the 64 ms guaranteed retention. The controller skips refresh, or uses partial-array refresh, for banks holding only such data. Linux patch, controller firmware and FPGA demo, ~$600k in 24 months.
why: Fact 3: recovers the 10-20% refresh bandwidth and refresh energy on the large share of AI memory that is short-lived.

title: Sourdough mother-culture: reference cells that age exactly like data
idea: Like a baker feeding a starter alongside every batch, each mat keeps two reference columns that are rewritten to '1' and '0' at every refresh. On activate they charge-share into a reference that has leaked exactly as much as the data cells since their last refresh.
why: A self-tracking reference removes temperature and time drift and recovers ~20% margin near the end of the refresh window (~1.5x longer refresh) with simple 180 nm circuitry.
